newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN denies Iraq request for added oil deal volumes.
newsitem.headline: UN denies Iraq request for added oil deal volumes.

text.p: A request by Iraq to add the cost of production and transportation to the amount of oil it can sell under the U.N. oil-for-food deal was rejected by the U.N. Security Council sanctions panel Tuesday.
German ambassador Tono Eitel, chair of the sanctions committee on Iraq, said the Iraqi request was denied on the advice of the U.N. legal department.
"Based on that, we said no," Eitel said.

Terms of the May 20 memorandum of understanding between Iraq and the United Nations allow Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil over a six-month period on a renewable basis. Around two-thirds of the oil funds are earmarked for food and aid purchases to ease the suffering of Iraqi civilians, caused by crippling sanctions imposed on Iraq after it invaded Kuwait in 1990.
The oil sales represent a partial lifting of those sanctions, meant for purely humanitarian purposes.
Eitel said among other matters discussed in the Tuesday sanctions panel meeting were Turkish requests to repair pipelines that will transport Iraqi oil for export under the oil-for-food scheme.

Turkey asked for permission to ship spare parts to Iraq to repair the Kirkuk-Yumutralik pipeline for both short-term and long-term needs. The sanctions panel approved shipments only for the short-term, and said it would review the long-term needs once the oil deal was operational, Eitel said.
Iraqi oil flows await final approval by U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali in the form of a "final report" to be submitted to the security council.
Diplomats and U.N. officials were expecting the report in December, possibly as early as December 10-15.
Inspectors from the Dutch-firm Saybolt are in Iraq, preparing to inspect oil metering stations, thought to the be the last technical hurdle standing in the way of oil sales.
